passages.text: Early blight of tomato is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Symptoms first appear on the older, lower leaves as small, dark brown to black spots (1-2 mm). These spots enlarge and develop characteristic concentric rings forming a target-like pattern. A yellow halo often surrounds the lesion. As the disease progresses, leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely. Stem lesions are dark and slightly sunken. Fruit symptoms appear as dark, leathery, sunken spots near the stem end.
passages.distinguishing_symptom: Concentric ring (target-like) pattern on leaf spots with yellow halo, starting from lower/older leaves
passages.prevention: Crop rotation (2-3 years), remove infected plant debris, use certified disease-free seeds, ensure adequate plant spacing for air circulation.
passages.source_document: TODO_VERIFY - ICAR Technical Bulletin / CIBRC Manual

passages.text: Late blight of tomato is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. The disease appears as large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions on leaves that rapidly turn dark brown to purplish-black. In humid conditions, white fuzzy sporulation is visible on the underside of leaves at the lesion margins. Stems develop dark brown to black lesions. Infected fruits show large, firm, brown, greasy-looking spots. The disease spreads extremely rapidly in cool, wet weather (15-25°C with high humidity).
passages.distinguishing_symptom: Large water-soaked lesions turning dark with white fuzzy growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions; very rapid spread
passages.prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation, destroy volunteer plants and cull piles, use resistant varieties, plant in well-drained soil.
passages.source_document: TODO_VERIFY - ICAR Technical Bulletin / CIBRC Manual

passages.text: Early blight of potato, caused by Alternaria solani, produces dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings on older leaves first. Lesions are typically angular and bounded by leaf veins. As the disease progresses, affected leaves become chlorotic, dry out, and may defoliate. Tuber infection causes shallow, dark, circular to irregular lesions on the skin, often with a slightly raised border. The underlying flesh is dry, corky, and brown. Disease is favored by warm temperatures (24-29°C) and alternating wet and dry periods.
passages.distinguishing_symptom: Lesions with concentric rings on older leaves, angular shape bounded by veins; tuber skin has shallow dark dry lesions
passages.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers, maintain adequate nutrition (especially potassium), practice crop rotation, remove volunteer plants.
passages.source_document: TODO_VERIFY - ICAR Technical Bulletin / CIBRC Manual

passages.text: Late blight of potato, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the most destructive disease of potato worldwide. Initial symptoms are water-soaked, pale green spots at leaf tips or margins that rapidly enlarge and turn dark brown to black. White sporulation appears on the lower leaf surface in humid conditions. Stems show dark brown lesions. Infected tubers have irregular, slightly depressed areas on the surface with a reddish-brown, granular rot extending into the flesh. Disease develops rapidly under cool (10-20°C), moist conditions with high humidity.
passages.distinguishing_symptom: Water-soaked spots at leaf tips/margins turning black; white sporulation underneath; tuber shows reddish-brown granular rot
passages.prevention: Use certified seed, hill potatoes properly, destroy cull piles, avoid irrigation during cool wet periods, apply preventive fungicides before disease onset.
passages.source_document: TODO_VERIFY - ICAR Technical Bulletin / CIBRC Manual

passages.text: Black rot of grape is caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. Leaf symptoms begin as small, yellowish spots that enlarge to form roughly circular, reddish-brown lesions (2-10 mm diameter) with a distinct dark brown to black margin. Tiny black pycnidia (fungal fruiting bodies) are visible within the lesion. On berries, a light-colored spot appears first, then the berry turns brown, shrivels, and becomes a hard, black, wrinkled mummy. Tendrils and shoots may also show elongated, dark, sunken cankers. Warm, wet weather (21-32°C) favors infection.
passages.distinguishing_symptom: Berries turn brown then shrivel into hard black wrinkled mummies; leaf spots have tiny black dots (pycnidia) inside
passages.prevention: Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected plant debris, prune for good air circulation, apply fungicides from bud break through veraison.
passages.source_document: TODO_VERIFY - ICAR Technical Bulletin / CIBRC Manual

passages.text: Common rust of maize is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. The disease is characterized by small (1-3 mm), elongated, brick-red to dark reddish-brown pustules (uredinia) that erupt through the leaf surface on both upper and lower sides. Pustules are scattered across the leaf and may coalesce in severe infections. Rubbing a finger over the pustules releases powdery, rust-colored spores. Late in the season, pustules may turn dark brown to black (telia stage). Heavily infected leaves may yellow and senesce prematurely. Cool to moderate temperatures (16-23°C) and high humidity or dew favor disease development.
passages.distinguishing_symptom: Small brick-red powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces that release rust-colored spores when rubbed
passages.prevention: Plant resistant hybrids, early planting to avoid peak spore periods, scout fields regularly from V8 to tasseling.
passages.source_document: TODO_VERIFY - ICAR Technical Bulletin / CIBRC Manual
